name: Chronic hepatitis B

triage.action: Discuss with your doctor at a routine appointment

name: Chronic hepatitis C

triage.action: Discuss with your doctor at a routine appointment

name: NAFLD (non-alcoholic fatty liver disease)

triage.label: Routine
triage.action: Discuss with your doctor at a routine appointment

Fibrosis staging (FIB-4, fibroscan) to identify the minority needing specialist follow-up

name: Bladder cancer

triage.label: See a doctor soon
triage.action: Arrange an appointment in the next day or two

Radical cystectomy or chemoradiotherapy for muscle-invasive disease

name: Urinary incontinence

triage.label: Routine
triage.action: Discuss with your doctor at a routine appointment

summary: Involuntary leakage of urine -- stress incontinence (leakage with coughing, sneezing or exertion, common after childbirth) or urge incontinence (a sudden strong urge with leakage before reaching the toilet, often with frequency). Urinalysis to exclude infection
Post-void residual measurement
Pelvic floor physiotherapy first-line for stress incontinence
Bladder training and antimuscarinics/beta-3 agonists for urge incontinence
Urodynamics if diagnosis unclear or surgery being considered

Urine culture
Scrotal ultrasound with Doppler to confirm blood flow and exclude torsion
Antibiotics per likely organism (STI-cover in younger sexually active men, coliform-cover in older men with urinary pathology)
Analgesia and scrotal support

name: Erectile dysfunction

triage.action: Discuss with your doctor at a routine appointment

PDE5 inhibitors first-line
Further options (vacuum devices, injections, surgery) if needed
Cardiovascular and diabetes risk assessment, especially in younger men with new-onset ED

name: Hydrocele

triage.action: Discuss with your doctor at a routine appointment

name: Bipolar affective disorder

triage.label: See a doctor soon

labs.confirms: Usually sufficient when the pattern is classic and examination is otherwise normal
Excludes vascular compression of the trigeminal nerve or a secondary structural cause

name: Trigeminal neuralgia

triage.label: Routine
triage.action: Discuss with your doctor at a routine appointment

summary: Sudden, severe, brief electric-shock-like facial pain in one or more trigeminal branches, triggered by touch, chewing, cold wind or brushing teeth. Frequently misdiagnosed initially as dental pain, leading to unnecessary dental procedures before the correct diagnosis is made -- worth considering explicitly before assuming a tooth problem. Sensory loss, symptoms on both sides, or onset under 40 should prompt MRI to exclude a structural cause (e.g. multiple sclerosis, a tumour) rather than assuming classical trigeminal neuralgia.
workup: Usually a clinical diagnosis from the classic pattern
MRI to exclude vascular compression or a secondary structural cause, especially if atypical
Carbamazepine is first-line and often dramatically effective
Surgical options (microvascular decompression, ablative procedures) if medically refractory

exam.positive: Essential tremor is worse with action and settles at rest -- the opposite pattern to Parkinson's classic rest tremor
Their presence points to Parkinson's disease rather than essential tremor -- worth checking explicitly rather than assuming

exam.step: Ask about a family history of tremor
exam.positive: Essential tremor is often familial, which can help reassure and distinguish it clinically

labs.confirms: Sufficient in a typical case with a normal neurological exam otherwise
Excludes hyperthyroidism as a contributing or alternative cause

name: Essential tremor

triage.label: Routine
triage.action: Discuss with your doctor at a routine appointment

summary: Fine, fast action tremor of the hands -- worse with movement or holding a posture, better at rest -- sometimes involving the voice or head, often with a family history. A common, benign cause of hand tremor that deserves clear differentiation from Parkinson's disease so patients aren't alarmed unnecessarily. Rest tremor, bradykinesia (slowness) or rigidity point to Parkinson's disease instead -- the two are commonly confused and worth distinguishing clearly.
workup: Usually a clinical diagnosis based on tremor characteristics and family history
Consider thyroid function tests to exclude hyperthyroidism as a contributor
Propranolol or primidone first-line if functionally troublesome
Botulinum toxin or, rarely, surgical options for refractory cases

exam.step: Ask about a diarrhoeal or respiratory illness in the last 1-3 weeks
exam.positive: A classic antecedent trigger, especially Campylobacter-associated diarrhoea, common in India

exam.step: Check reflexes and the pattern of weakness -- ascending, symmetrical
exam.positive: Reduced or absent reflexes with symmetrical, ascending weakness is the hallmark pattern, distinct from a single-limb or asymmetric cause

exam.step: Ask specifically about breathlessness or difficulty swallowing
exam.positive: Either indicates respiratory muscle involvement -- a medical emergency needing urgent admission for monitoring, not routine outpatient follow-up

labs.confirms: Albuminocytological dissociation (raised protein, normal cell count) supports the diagnosis, though it may be normal in the first week
Shows the demyelinating pattern characteristic of GBS
Tracks respiratory muscle involvement -- a falling trend is the trigger for ICU-level monitoring/ventilatory support

name: Guillain-Barre syndrome

triage.label: Urgent
triage.action: Seek medical assessment today

summary: Progressive, ascending, symmetrical limb weakness over days, often following a diarrhoeal or respiratory infection 1-3 weeks earlier, with reduced or absent reflexes. A genuine not-to-miss emergency -- Campylobacter-associated GBS in particular follows the diarrhoeal illnesses common in India, so a recent diarrhoea history plus new limb weakness should raise this immediately. Breathlessness, difficulty swallowing, or rapidly progressing weakness indicate respiratory muscle involvement -- a medical emergency needing urgent admission for monitoring.
workup: Lumbar puncture (raised CSF protein with a normal cell count -- albuminocytological dissociation)
Nerve conduction studies
Monitor forced vital capacity closely
IVIG or plasma exchange in a monitored (often ICU) setting
Supportive care including ventilatory support if needed
Physiotherapy in recovery

exam.step: Ask specifically how long symptoms have been present
exam.positive: Persistence beyond 12 weeks is the defining feature separating this from acute sinusitis, which settles within a few weeks
Reduced or lost smell is a genuine, common feature of chronic disease, more so than in a typical acute episode

exam.step: Check whether symptoms are one-sided, or whether there is blood-stained discharge or any visual/neurological symptom
exam.positive: Any of these should prompt imaging to exclude a structural or malignant cause rather than assuming simple chronic sinusitis

labs.confirms: Directly visualises mucosal changes, polyps or discharge
Shows the extent of mucosal disease -- reserved for surgical planning or diagnostic uncertainty, not routine
Identifies a treatable allergic driver if suspected

name: Chronic rhinosinusitis

triage.label: Routine
triage.action: Discuss with your doctor at a routine appointment

summary: Nasal blockage, thick nasal discharge, facial pressure/pain and reduced sense of smell, persisting beyond 12 weeks -- distinct from ordinary acute sinusitis, which settles much sooner. Air pollution and the high ambient allergen/dust load in many Indian cities are relevant chronic drivers worth asking about alongside standard advice. Unilateral symptoms with blood-stained discharge, or visual/neurological symptoms, should prompt imaging to exclude a structural or malignant cause rather than assuming simple chronic sinusitis.
workup: Nasal endoscopy
CT sinuses if surgery being considered or diagnosis unclear
Allergy testing if an allergic component is suspected
Saline irrigation and intranasal corticosteroid are first-line and often very effective
Longer antibiotic courses or oral steroids for flares
Endoscopic sinus surgery for refractory disease/nasal polyps

exam.step: Ask exactly how the bleeding was managed and for how long
exam.positive: Correctly applied pressure (soft part of the nose, 15-20 minutes, leaning forward, not lying back) fails to stop far less often than incorrectly applied pressure

exam.step: Ask about blood-thinning medication and high blood pressure
exam.positive: Both are recognised contributing factors and change how aggressively to investigate and manage recurrent bleeds

exam.step: Ask whether blood is also being felt/tasted at the back of the throat despite front-of-nose pressure
exam.positive: Suggests posterior epistaxis -- needs urgent ENT assessment, not standard first aid alone

labs.test: Clinical assessment and blood pressure check
labs.confirms: Sufficient for a single, minor, self-limiting bleed

labs.test: Full blood count and clotting screen
labs.confirms: Reserved for recurrent, severe, or anticoagulant-related bleeding

name: Epistaxis (nosebleed)

triage.label: Self-care
triage.action: This can usually be managed at home

summary: Bleeding from the nose, most commonly from Little's area at the front of the septum -- often triggered by dry air, nose picking/trauma, or in the context of high blood pressure or blood-thinning medication. Genuinely common, especially in the dry season, and highly amenable to clear first-aid self-care. Heavy, prolonged bleeding not controlled by 15-20 minutes of correct first-aid pressure, or bleeding from the back of the nose (posterior epistaxis), needs urgent ENT assessment.
workup: Usually a clinical diagnosis
Check blood pressure
Full blood count and clotting if recurrent, severe, or on blood thinners
Firm continuous pressure on the soft part of the nose for a full 15-20 minutes, leaning forward
Nasal cautery or packing if first aid fails
Treat underlying high blood pressure or a clotting problem if found

exam.step: Ask whether hearing loss came on gradually over time, or suddenly
exam.positive: A gradual reduction is typical of wax; sudden hearing loss is NOT typical and needs separate, prompt assessment

exam.step: Ask about ear pain, discharge, or vertigo
exam.positive: None of these are typical of simple wax impaction -- their presence should prompt a different assessment, not reassurance

exam.step: Otoscopy to directly visualise the ear canal
exam.positive: Confirms wax occluding the view of the eardrum -- the definitive bedside finding

labs.confirms: Directly visualises occluding wax against the eardrum -- confirms the diagnosis at the bedside

name: Ear wax impaction

triage.label: Self-care
triage.action: This can usually be managed at home

summary: Gradual reduction in hearing, a sensation of blockage or fullness in the ear, sometimes mild discomfort or ringing -- very common and entirely benign. One of the most common, entirely benign causes of reduced hearing in any clinic, easily missed when a checker only routes reduced hearing to serious causes like Meniere's disease or otitis media. Sudden hearing loss, pain, discharge or vertigo are NOT typical of simple wax impaction and need separate assessment.
workup: Otoscopy confirms visible occluding wax
Ear drops (olive oil or sodium bicarbonate) to soften the wax
Irrigation or microsuction if not cleared by drops alone
Avoid cotton buds, which often push wax further in

exam.step: Ask specifically whether the pain is sharp and tearing, and whether it comes ON with defecation
exam.positive: This sharp, defecation-triggered pain is the key feature distinguishing a fissure from haemorrhoids, which are typically far less painful

exam.step: Gently part the buttocks to look for a visible tear at the anal margin
exam.positive: Usually visible without internal examination, which is often too painful to perform acutely

exam.step: Check whether the fissure is midline, single, and healing
exam.positive: Fissures off the midline, multiple, or not healing should raise suspicion of Crohn's disease, TB or malignancy rather than a simple fissure

labs.confirms: Usually sufficient -- a visible tear at the anal margin, typically posterior midline

name: Anal fissure

triage.label: Self-care
triage.action: This can usually be managed at home

summary: Sharp, severe pain on defecation, often with a small amount of bright red blood on the paper, and a visible tear at the anal margin -- frequently after a hard stool. Very common and frequently confused with haemorrhoids by patients -- the sharp pain-on-defecation pattern (haemorrhoids are typically far less painful, if painful at all) is the key distinguishing feature. Fissures that are off the midline, multiple, or non-healing should raise suspicion of Crohn's disease, TB or malignancy rather than a simple fissure.
workup: Usually clinical (visual inspection)
Examination under anaesthesia/biopsy if atypical
Stool softeners and a high-fibre diet
Topical GTN or diltiazem to relax the sphincter
Botulinum toxin injection or sphincterotomy if chronic/resistant

exam.step: Ask specifically about a sudden deceleration injury (road traffic collision, fall)
exam.positive: The defining precipitant -- absence of one should prompt reconsidering the diagnosis

exam.step: Check for arm weakness, numbness, or midline cervical spine tenderness after significant trauma
exam.positive: Any of these need imaging to exclude a fracture or cord injury before labelling this simple whiplash

exam.positive: Determines objectively whether imaging is needed, rather than imaging everyone or no one

labs.confirms: Validated decision rule for whether imaging is needed -- avoids both over- and under-investigation
Excludes fracture or instability when red flags or the clinical rule indicate it

name: Whiplash injury

triage.label: Self-care
triage.action: This can usually be managed at home

summary: Neck pain and stiffness developing hours to a day after a sudden deceleration injury -- classically a road traffic collision -- sometimes with headache or arm symptoms. Road-traffic-collision rates and injury patterns are high in India, so this is worth considering explicitly given the volume of minor-collision neck injuries seen in routine practice. Neurological symptoms (arm weakness/numbness), or midline cervical spine tenderness after significant trauma, need imaging to exclude a fracture or cord injury before this is labelled simple whiplash.
workup: Clinical assessment against a validated rule (e.g. Canadian C-spine rule) to decide if imaging is needed
Plain X-ray/CT if red flags are present
Early mobilisation and physiotherapy -- genuinely better outcomes than prolonged collar immobilisation
Analgesia as needed

exam.step: Ask whether pain is worse with thumb movement or gripping, and about recent repetitive lifting (e.g. a new baby)
exam.positive: The classic pattern -- worse with thumb/wrist use, often in new mothers or repetitive manual work

exam.step: Palpate directly over the tendons at the base of the thumb for tenderness and swelling
exam.positive: Localised tenderness over the first extensor compartment is the key finding

exam.step: Perform Finkelstein's test (thumb tucked into fist, wrist deviated toward the little finger)
exam.positive: Reproduces the pain -- the classic bedside diagnostic manoeuvre

labs.confirms: Positive test (pain reproduced) is usually sufficient for clinical diagnosis
Confirms tendon sheath thickening/swelling if the diagnosis is unclear

name: De Quervain's tenosynovitis

triage.label: Self-care
triage.action: This can usually be managed at home

summary: Pain and swelling at the base of the thumb/wrist, worse with thumb movement or gripping -- classically in new mothers (lifting an infant) or repetitive manual work. A genuinely frequent, easily-missed cause of 'wrist pain', common in new mothers given typical infant-carrying/lifting patterns and in manual/agricultural workers. Persistent swelling with systemic joint symptoms should prompt consideration of inflammatory arthritis instead, not more of the same self-care advice.
workup: Clinical diagnosis (a positive Finkelstein's test)
Ultrasound if diagnosis unclear
Splinting and activity modification
NSAIDs
Corticosteroid injection if not settling
Surgical release rarely needed for resistant cases

exam.step: Look for honey-coloured, crusted sores, typically around the nose/mouth or on exposed limbs
exam.positive: The classic, near-diagnostic appearance -- no dedicated evidence node captures this crust colour/texture directly, so it is assessed visually

exam.step: Ask about a preceding skin break, insect bite, or underlying eczema
exam.positive: A very common predisposing factor -- impetigo classically follows a break in the skin's barrier

exam.step: Check for fever or signs of the child being systemically unwell
exam.positive: Usually absent in simple impetigo -- its presence should raise concern for cellulitis or a more serious complication instead

labs.confirms: Usually sufficient given the characteristic appearance
Reserved for recurrent, extensive, or treatment-resistant cases, to guide antibiotic choice

name: Impetigo

triage.label: Self-care
triage.action: This can usually be managed at home

summary: A highly contagious superficial bacterial skin infection, classically producing honey-coloured, crusted sores -- usually on the face or limbs -- most common in children, and often following a minor break in the skin (an insect bite, graze, or eczema). Spreads readily to other skin sites and to close contacts by direct touch or shared towels/clothing, so hygiene advice matters as much as treatment. Widespread involvement, fever, or a child who is systemically unwell should raise concern for cellulitis or, rarely, a more serious streptococcal complication rather than simple impetigo.
workup: Usually a clinical diagnosis on the appearance of the lesions
Skin swab for culture if recurrent, extensive, or not responding to treatment
Topical antibiotic (e.g. fusidic acid/mupirocin) for limited disease
Oral antibiotics if widespread or bullous
Exclude from school/childcare until lesions are crusted over or 24-48 hours of antibiotics have been completed

exam.step: Inspect for a rough, hyperkeratotic surface, often with small black dots (thrombosed capillaries)
exam.positive: The classic appearance -- no dedicated evidence node captures this texture directly, so it is assessed visually

exam.step: Ask whether it itches or has changed rapidly in size, colour or shape
exam.positive: Warts are typically non-itchy and slow-changing -- rapid change or itch should prompt reconsidering the diagnosis

exam.step: Ask about the number and distribution of lesions, and any history of immunosuppression
exam.positive: Unusually numerous or resistant warts can be a sign of underlying immunosuppression

labs.confirms: Usually sufficient given the characteristic appearance
Reserved for atypical, rapidly-changing, or diagnostically uncertain lesions to exclude another cause

name: Warts (viral)

triage.label: Self-care
triage.action: This can usually be managed at home

summary: A rough, raised, skin-coloured lesion caused by HPV infection of the skin -- common on the hands and feet (where pressure can make plantar warts painful to walk on) -- usually painless, non-itchy, and slow to change, persisting for months. Common in children and young adults, and spreads by direct skin contact or shared surfaces (communal showers, swimming pools). More numerous or treatment-resistant warts can be a sign of underlying immunosuppression and should prompt that consideration rather than repeated cosmetic treatment alone.
workup: Usually a clinical diagnosis on appearance
Watchful waiting -- most resolve spontaneously within 1-2 years, especially in children
Topical salicylic acid
Cryotherapy (liquid nitrogen) for resistant lesions
Consider an immunosuppression work-up if warts are unusually numerous, large, or resistant to treatment

exam.step: Inspect for small, dome-shaped, flesh-coloured papules with a central dimple (umbilication)
exam.positive: The classic near-diagnostic appearance -- no dedicated evidence node captures the central umbilication directly, so it is assessed visually

exam.step: Ask about surrounding itchy, eczema-like skin
exam.positive: A halo of dermatitis around lesions is common, especially in children with an atopic background

exam.step: Ask about the extent and persistence of lesions, especially in an adult
exam.positive: Unusually extensive or persistent molluscum can be a marker of underlying immunosuppression, including undiagnosed HIV

labs.confirms: Usually sufficient given the characteristic appearance
Reserved for diagnostically uncertain or atypical lesions

name: Molluscum contagiosum

triage.label: Self-care
triage.action: This can usually be managed at home

summary: Small, dome-shaped, flesh-coloured papules, often with a central dimple (umbilication), caused by a poxvirus -- common in children and spread by direct skin contact, shared towels/bathwater, or (in adults) sexually. Usually painless and mildly itchy at most, self-limiting over months to around a year, though lesions often multiply before they clear. Unusually extensive or persistent molluscum, especially in an adult, can be a marker of underlying immunosuppression (including undiagnosed HIV) and should prompt that consideration.
workup: Usually a clinical diagnosis on appearance
Watchful waiting -- most resolve spontaneously within 6-18 months
Physical removal (curettage or cryotherapy) if lesions are troublesome or cosmetically bothersome
Consider an immunosuppression/HIV work-up if lesions are unusually extensive, large, or persistent, particularly in an adult

exam.step: Inspect the scalp, eyebrows, nasolabial folds and behind the ears for greasy, yellowish scale on mild redness
exam.positive: The classic distribution and appearance

exam.step: Ask about a waxing/waning course with stress or seasonal triggers
exam.positive: A relapsing-remitting pattern is typical, distinguishing it from a one-off acute rash

exam.step: Ask about the extent and treatment-resistance, especially in an adult
exam.positive: Unusually severe or resistant seborrhoeic dermatitis can be a marker of underlying immunosuppression

labs.confirms: Usually sufficient given the characteristic distribution and appearance
Reserved for atypical or diagnostically uncertain presentations

name: Seborrhoeic dermatitis

triage.label: Self-care
triage.action: This can usually be managed at home

summary: Greasy, yellowish scaling on a mildly red base, classically on the scalp, eyebrows, sides of the nose and behind the ears -- a chronic, relapsing-remitting condition linked to an inflammatory reaction to Malassezia yeast naturally living on the skin, not a true infection. Flares are often triggered by stress, cold weather, or reduced skin care. Mild hair thinning can occur over affected scalp areas. Widespread, unusually severe or treatment-resistant seborrhoeic dermatitis, especially in an adult, can be a marker of underlying immunosuppression (including undiagnosed HIV) and should prompt that consideration.
workup: Usually a clinical diagnosis on appearance and distribution
Topical antifungal (ketoconazole or ciclopirox) shampoo/cream
Topical mild corticosteroid for flares
Regular, ongoing use of medicated shampoo to prevent recurrence -- this is a chronic, relapsing condition, not a one-off cure

exam.step: Inspect for well-defined, milky-white patches, checking under Wood's lamp if available
exam.positive: Wood's lamp examination confirms and defines the true extent of depigmentation

exam.step: Ask specifically whether the patches itch, hurt, or have any scale
exam.positive: Vitiligo is classically asymptomatic -- genuine itch, pain or scale should prompt reconsidering the diagnosis

exam.step: Ask about a family or personal history of autoimmune conditions, especially thyroid disease
exam.positive: Vitiligo is genuinely associated with other autoimmune conditions, particularly autoimmune thyroid disease

labs.confirms: Confirms the diagnosis and defines the true extent of depigmented skin
Screens for the genuinely associated autoimmune thyroid disease

name: Vitiligo

triage.label: Routine
triage.action: Discuss with your doctor at a routine appointment

summary: Well-defined, milky-white patches of skin caused by loss of pigment-producing melanocytes -- classically asymptomatic (no itch, pain or scale), slowly progressive, and often starting around the hands, face, or body folds. An autoimmune-associated condition, not infectious or contagious -- an important reassurance point, since the visible appearance is often mistaken by patients or others for a contagious skin infection. Rapidly changing pigment loss, or pigment loss with genuine itch/scale, should prompt reconsidering the diagnosis rather than assuming vitiligo.
workup: Usually a clinical diagnosis on appearance
Wood's lamp examination to confirm and define extent
Screen for associated autoimmune conditions (thyroid disease in particular)
Topical corticosteroids or calcineurin inhibitors
Phototherapy (narrowband UVB) for more extensive disease

exam.step: Examine the pattern: diffuse thinning vs well-defined round patches of complete hair loss
exam.positive: Distinguishes androgenetic alopecia (diffuse, gradual) from alopecia areata (patchy, often sudden) -- no dedicated evidence node captures this pattern directly, so it is assessed visually

exam.positive: Their presence points away from simple alopecia toward a systemic cause (thyroid disease, iron deficiency) that needs its own work-up

exam.positive: Excessive hairs coming away easily suggests active, ongoing shedding rather than a stable pattern

labs.confirms: Screens for the two most common treatable systemic causes of hair loss when other symptoms are present
Helps distinguish androgenetic alopecia from alopecia areata and other causes when the pattern is unclear

name: Alopecia

triage.label: Routine
triage.action: Discuss with your doctor at a routine appointment

summary: Hair thinning or loss without another systemic illness driving it -- either gradual, diffuse thinning following a male/female pattern (androgenetic alopecia), or sudden, well-defined round patches of complete hair loss (alopecia areata, an autoimmune condition). These two patterns are clinically distinct but both present as 'hair loss' to a symptom checker -- no dedicated evidence node distinguishes patchy/sudden from diffuse/ gradual hair loss, so this is assessed on examination. Hair loss WITH other symptoms (fatigue, weight change, cold intolerance) points away from simple alopecia toward a systemic cause (thyroid disease, iron deficiency) instead, and should be investigated as such.

Screen for an underlying systemic cause (ferritin, TSH) if there are any other symptoms
Topical minoxidil for androgenetic alopecia
Topical or intralesional corticosteroids for alopecia areata
Dermatology referral for extensive, rapidly progressive, or diagnostically uncertain hair loss

exam.step: Inspect for a pearly/waxy bump, a persistent scaly patch, or a sore that bleeds and doesn't heal, on sun-exposed skin
exam.positive: The classic pattern -- warrants prompt assessment rather than reassurance

exam.step: Ask specifically how long the lesion has been present and whether it has changed, bled, or failed to heal
exam.positive: Slow growth over months to years with bleeding or non-healing is the concerning pattern, distinct from an acute infection

exam.step: Assess sun-exposure history and skin type
exam.positive: Cumulative sun exposure and fair skin are the dominant risk factors, especially in older adults

labs.confirms: Aids clinical diagnosis and helps decide which lesions need biopsy
Definitive diagnosis for any clinically suspicious lesion -- should not be delayed

name: Skin cancer (non-melanoma)

triage.label: Urgent
triage.action: Seek medical assessment today

summary: A slow-growing, often painless skin lesion -- a pearly or waxy bump, a persistent scaly patch, or a sore that bleeds easily and doesn't fully heal -- developing over months to years, usually on sun-exposed skin (face, ears, scalp, hands) in older adults. Actinic keratosis (rough, scaly, sun-damage patches) is a precursor that can progress to squamous cell carcinoma if untreated. Any new or changing skin lesion in this pattern -- especially one that bleeds, doesn't heal, or is enlarging -- needs prompt clinical assessment and often a biopsy, not reassurance or watchful waiting.
workup: Prompt clinical assessment -- do not delay for a lesion matching this pattern
Dermoscopy
Biopsy of any clinically suspicious lesion
Surgical excision or other definitive treatment once confirmed, per the specific diagnosis and risk category

exam.step: Look inside the cheeks for Koplik's spots (tiny white-grey spots on a red background)
exam.positive: The single most specific early sign, present in 60-70% of cases -- no dedicated evidence node captures this directly, so it is assessed visually

exam.step: Confirm the classic sequence: fever and the '3 Cs' (cough, coryza, conjunctivitis) preceding the rash by 2-4 days
exam.positive: This sequence, and the rash spreading from the face downward, is the classic pattern

exam.step: Check vaccination status and any known exposure/outbreak
exam.positive: Measles occurs almost exclusively in unvaccinated or under-vaccinated individuals

labs.confirms: Confirms the diagnosis, particularly important given its notifiable-disease and public-health status
Often sufficient in a known outbreak with the classic clinical picture

name: Measles

triage.label: Self-care
triage.action: This can usually be managed at home

summary: A highly contagious viral illness starting with high fever, cough, runny nose and conjunctivitis (the classic '3 Cs') 2-4 days before a red-brown, blotchy rash spreads from the face down the body. Koplik's spots -- tiny white-grey spots on the inside of the cheeks -- are the single most specific early sign but appear in only 60-70% of cases and are not captured by a dedicated evidence node here, so this is assessed on examination. Occurs in unvaccinated or under-vaccinated individuals of any age, not just children. Serious complications (pneumonia, encephalitis) are genuinely more common than in most other childhood exanthems, so this should never be dismissed as 'just a rash'.
workup: Usually a clinical diagnosis, supported by measles IgM/PCR testing
Notify public health -- measles is a notifiable disease in most jurisdictions
Supportive care (fluids, antipyretics)
Vitamin A supplementation per WHO guidance, which reduces complication severity
Isolation until 4 days after rash onset to limit spread

exam.step: Palpate behind the ears and at the back of the neck for swollen glands
exam.positive: Postauricular/suboccipital lymphadenopathy is a genuine distinguishing feature from measles

exam.step: Ask about joint aches, especially in adult women
exam.positive: A real, commonly-taught feature of rubella, more prominent than in most other childhood exanthems

exam.step: Always ask about pregnancy status, in the patient or a close contact
exam.positive: First-trimester infection risks congenital rubella syndrome -- this changes the urgency of the assessment, even though the illness itself is usually mild

labs.confirms: Confirms the diagnosis, particularly important for pregnancy risk assessment and public-health notification
Often sufficient with the classic clinical picture in a non-pregnant, non-exposed context

name: Rubella

triage.label: Self-care
triage.action: This can usually be managed at home

summary: A generally milder viral illness than measles -- a fine, pink rash spreading from the face down the body over about 3 days, with mild fever and characteristic postauricular/suboccipital lymphadenopathy (swollen glands behind the ears and at the back of the neck), a genuine distinguishing feature from measles. Joint aches are common, especially in adult women. The critical clinical point: infection in the first trimester of pregnancy can cause congenital rubella syndrome (deafness, cataracts, heart defects) in the baby -- any suspected rubella in a pregnant woman or her contacts needs prompt assessment for this reason, not for the mother's own mild illness.
workup: Usually a clinical diagnosis, supported by rubella IgM/PCR testing
Notify public health -- rubella is a notifiable disease in most jurisdictions
Urgent assessment if a pregnant woman is exposed or affected, because of congenital rubella syndrome risk to the baby
Supportive care (fluids, antipyretics) -- the illness itself is usually mild and self-limiting

exam.step: Palpate for swelling of the parotid gland, in front of and below the ear, obscuring the angle of the jaw
exam.positive: The defining feature -- no dedicated evidence node captures parotid swelling directly, so it is assessed on examination

exam.step: Ask specifically about testicular pain or swelling in a post-pubertal male, or abdominal pain
exam.positive: Orchitis and pancreatitis are genuine, clinically important complications worth actively asking about, not just the parotid swelling itself

exam.step: Check vaccination status and any known exposure/outbreak
exam.positive: Mumps occurs mainly in unvaccinated or under-vaccinated individuals

labs.confirms: Often sufficient given the characteristic parotid swelling in a known exposure/outbreak

labs.test: Mumps IgM serology, PCR, or salivary swab
labs.confirms: Confirms the diagnosis when uncertain, particularly important for public-health notification

name: Mumps

triage.label: Self-care
triage.action: This can usually be managed at home

summary: A viral illness with a prodrome of fever, headache and malaise, followed by painful swelling of one or both parotid (salivary) glands, in front of and below the ear, over several days -- the defining feature, though no dedicated evidence node captures parotid swelling directly (it is a glandular swelling, not lymph-node swelling, and is assessed on examination). Occurs mainly in unvaccinated or under-vaccinated individuals. Complications genuinely include orchitis (testicular swelling/pain, particularly in post-pubertal males), pancreatitis, and rarely meningitis or hearing loss -- these should be actively asked about, not just the parotid swelling itself.
workup: Usually a clinical diagnosis on the characteristic parotid swelling
Notify public health -- mumps is a notifiable disease in most jurisdictions
Supportive care (fluids, antipyretics, warm/cold compresses to the swollen gland)
Ask specifically about testicular pain/swelling (orchitis), abdominal pain (pancreatitis), or severe headache/neck stiffness (meningitis) as possible complications

exam.step: Ask specifically about a characteristic inspiratory 'whoop' after coughing fits, or vomiting after coughing
exam.positive: Post-tussive vomiting and the whoop are real hallmarks -- no dedicated evidence node captures either directly, so this is assessed by history

exam.step: Ask how long the cough has lasted
exam.positive: A cough persisting for weeks, well beyond a typical viral illness, is characteristic -- the '100-day cough'
Fever is usually low-grade or absent in pertussis -- its prominent presence should raise suspicion of Croup, Bronchiolitis or pneumonia instead

labs.confirms: The standard confirmatory test, most sensitive in the first 2-3 weeks of illness
Reasonable in a known outbreak with the classic paroxysmal, prolonged cough pattern

name: Whooping cough

triage.label: Urgent
triage.action: Seek medical assessment today

summary: A prolonged, paroxysmal cough illness -- severe coughing fits, sometimes ending in a characteristic inspiratory 'whoop' or post-tussive vomiting (no dedicated evidence node captures the whoop or vomiting directly, carried in the exam narrative), lasting weeks to months (the '100-day cough'). Notably, fever is usually low-grade or absent -- a real distinguishing feature from Croup or Bronchiolitis, which typically have a more prominent fever. Occurs in unvaccinated/under-vaccinated children AND in adults with waning vaccine immunity, who can then transmit it to vulnerable unvaccinated infants -- the group at real risk of apnoea and severe complications.
workup: Nasopharyngeal swab PCR for Bordetella pertussis
Notify public health -- pertussis is a notifiable disease in most jurisdictions
A macrolide antibiotic (azithromycin 3-5 days, or clarithromycin/erythromycin) -- reduces transmission but does NOT shorten the illness once established, an honestly-nuanced point
Urgent assessment for any young infant with suspected pertussis, given real apnoea/complication risk
Ensure close contacts, especially pregnant women and young infants, are appropriately protected/vaccinated

exam.step: Wash the wound immediately with soap and running water for 15 minutes -- do this before anything else, including before seeking further care
exam.positive: The single most effective life-saving intervention, and it is entirely within the patient's own immediate control

exam.step: Categorise the exposure per WHO criteria (touching/feeding an animal = category I, no PEP; minor scratches without bleeding = category II; bites, broken skin, or mucous membrane contact = category III, needs RIG plus vaccine)
exam.positive: Determines exactly what treatment is needed -- not every animal contact needs the full regimen, but every category III exposure needs it started immediately

exam.step: Ask about the animal: was it a known, healthy, vaccinated pet available for observation, or a stray/wild animal that cannot be observed?
exam.positive: A healthy pet dog available for 10 days' observation changes the risk calculation, but PEP should still be started immediately and only stopped if the animal remains healthy throughout observation

labs.confirms: The basis for the PEP decision -- there is no diagnostic test that can safely rule out rabies exposure before symptoms develop

labs.test: Direct fluorescent antibody testing of the animal (if it dies/is euthanised)
labs.confirms: Can confirm or exclude rabies in the animal, but PEP should never be delayed waiting for this result

name: Rabies (animal bite exposure)

triage.label: Emergency
triage.action: Call emergency services or go to an emergency department now

summary: Any bite, scratch, or lick on broken skin/mucous membrane from a dog, cat, monkey or other mammal in a rabies-endemic area (including almost all of India) needs to be treated as a possible rabies exposure -- not diagnosed by waiting for symptoms. Once symptoms of rabies itself develop (agitation, hydrophobia, paralysis), the disease is essentially 100% fatal -- there is no treatment at that stage. This is why the response to a bite is about IMMEDIATE wound care and post-exposure prophylaxis, not observation. India accounts for the largest share of the world's human rabies deaths, almost entirely from dog bites, and almost entirely because prophylaxis was delayed, incomplete, or not started at all -- not because prophylaxis failed. No dedicated 'animal bite' evidence node exists in this checker; the wound itself is captured only as a generic open wound, assessed on history.
workup: Immediately wash the wound with soap and running water for a full 15 minutes -- the single most effective, cheapest life-saving step, and it works even hours later if not yet done
Start the WHO post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) vaccination schedule promptly -- do not wait for the animal to be observed or tested before starting
Rabies immunoglobulin (RIG) into and around the wound for category III exposures (broken skin, mucous membrane contact, or bites) per WHO categorisation
Complete the FULL vaccination course as scheduled -- partial/incomplete courses are a major, genuinely documented cause of preventable deaths
Tetanus prophylaxis and antibiotics for the wound itself, as for any bite wound

exam.positive: Often raised, but a meaningful proportion of chronic open-angle glaucoma has only mildly raised or normal IOP -- a real nuance, not a clean rule-out test on its own

exam.step: Ask specifically whether the eye is painful or red
exam.positive: Classically neither -- a painless, white eye is the key distinguishing feature from acute angle-closure glaucoma, which is the opposite on both counts

exam.step: Formal visual field testing and optic disc examination
exam.positive: Peripheral field loss and optic disc cupping are the actual diagnostic findings -- no dedicated evidence node captures peripheral vision loss directly here, so this is assessed on formal testing rather than the patient's own description

labs.confirms: Supportive but not always raised -- see the nuance above

labs.test: Formal visual field testing (perimetry) and optic disc imaging
labs.confirms: The actual diagnostic findings for glaucoma -- peripheral field loss and characteristic disc cupping

name: Chronic open-angle glaucoma

triage.label: See a doctor soon
triage.action: Arrange an appointment in the next day or two

summary: A slowly progressive, classically PAINLESS optic nerve disease with a white (not red), comfortable eye -- the exact opposite presentation to acute angle-closure glaucoma, which shares this bundle. Vision loss begins in the peripheral field and is often unnoticed by the patient until advanced, since the brain compensates -- no dedicated 'peripheral/tunnel vision' evidence node exists here, so this is assessed on formal visual field testing rather than the patient's own description of blur. Genuinely the most common form of glaucoma, far more common than the acute presentation, and a leading cause of irreversible blindness worldwide precisely because it is silent until late -- routine eye pressure screening after age 40, not waiting for symptoms, is the point.
workup: Intraocular pressure (IOP) measurement -- though a meaningful fraction of cases have only mildly raised or even normal IOP ('normal-tension glaucoma'), so a normal reading does not exclude it
Formal visual field testing -- detects the characteristic peripheral field loss well before the patient notices it
Optic disc examination/imaging for characteristic cupping
Topical IOP-lowering eye drops (prostaglandin analogues first-line)
Laser trabeculoplasty or surgery if drops are insufficient

exam.step: Ask specifically whether the pain is tightly tied to the menstrual cycle (starts with or just before bleeding, eases within a few days)
exam.positive: The defining pattern of primary dysmenorrhoea -- pain outside this window should prompt reconsidering the diagnosis

exam.step: Ask whether the pain has been progressively worsening over months, or is present outside the cyclical window
exam.positive: Either should raise suspicion of a secondary cause (such as endometriosis) rather than primary dysmenorrhoea

exam.step: General abdominal and pelvic examination to exclude tenderness/masses suggesting another cause
exam.positive: Primary dysmenorrhoea should have an otherwise normal examination

labs.confirms: Usually sufficient given the classic cyclical pattern in a young woman with an otherwise normal examination
Reserved for atypical presentations (non-cyclical pain, progressive worsening, treatment-resistant) to exclude a secondary cause

name: Dysmenorrhoea

triage.label: Self-care
triage.action: This can usually be managed at home

summary: Cramping lower abdominal/pelvic pain tightly tied to the menstrual cycle -- starting just before or with the onset of bleeding and easing over 1-3 days -- without an underlying pelvic disease (primary dysmenorrhoea). Extremely common, especially in the teens and twenties, and often under-discussed. Pain that is NOT confined to this cyclical window, that has been steadily worsening over months, or that is not relieved by usual measures should prompt considering a secondary cause (such as endometriosis) instead of assuming primary dysmenorrhoea.
workup: Usually a clinical diagnosis based on the cyclical pattern -- no investigation needed for typical primary dysmenorrhoea in a young woman
NSAIDs (e.g. mefenamic acid, ibuprofen), started at or just before the onset of pain -- genuinely effective, not just symptomatic cover
Hormonal contraception if NSAIDs alone are insufficient
Heat applied to the lower abdomen as a supportive measure
Pelvic ultrasound/referral if pain is not confined to the cyclical window, is progressively worsening, or not responding to standard treatment -- to exclude a secondary cause

exam.step: Ask whether pelvic pain is present at times OTHER than around menstruation, not just during it
exam.positive: A genuine distinguishing feature from primary dysmenorrhoea, where pain is confined to the cyclical window

exam.step: Ask how long the pain has been present and whether it has been progressively worsening
exam.positive: Chronic, gradually-established pain over months to years is the classic pattern, distinct from an acute new problem

exam.step: Pelvic examination for tenderness, nodularity, or reduced mobility of pelvic structures
exam.positive: Supportive findings, though a normal examination does not exclude endometriosis

labs.confirms: Can identify endometriomas (ovarian cysts from endometriosis) but a normal scan does not exclude the diagnosis
The definitive diagnostic and treatment step, reserved for confirmed/suspected cases needing certainty or surgical management

name: Endometriosis

triage.label: See a doctor soon
triage.action: Arrange an appointment in the next day or two

summary: Chronic pelvic pain from endometrial-type tissue growing outside the uterus -- classically worse around menstruation but, unlike simple dysmenorrhoea, often present at other times of the cycle too, and progressively established over months to years rather than a new, acute problem. Genuinely under-recognised and under-diagnosed -- diagnostic delay of several years and multiple healthcare visits before a correct diagnosis is well documented, including in India, so pain dismissed as 'just bad periods' deserves a second look if it is severe, chronic, or affecting daily life.
workup: Pelvic ultrasound (transvaginal where appropriate) -- can suggest but not definitively rule out endometriosis
Referral to gynaecology for further assessment if pain is severe or affecting daily life -- do not dismiss chronic pelvic pain as 'just periods'
Laparoscopy remains the definitive diagnostic and treatment step for confirmed/suspected cases
NSAIDs and hormonal treatment (combined pill, progestogens) as first-line medical management
Fertility assessment if trying to conceive, since endometriosis can affect fertility

exam.step: Ask about the site (usually one-sided), onset (gradual vs sudden), and any nausea/vomiting
exam.positive: Sudden severe one-sided pain with nausea/vomiting raises concern for ovarian torsion -- a surgical emergency needing urgent assessment, distinct from a simple cyst

exam.step: Ask where the patient is in her menstrual cycle and whether the pain relates to it
exam.positive: Functional cysts relate to normal ovulatory/luteal-phase activity, so timing in the cycle is a useful clue

exam.step: Abdominal and pelvic examination for a palpable mass or focal tenderness
exam.positive: May reveal a mass or tenderness over the affected ovary, though many cysts are not palpable

labs.confirms: The key investigation -- characterises size, structure (simple vs complex) and guides whether expectant management or referral is appropriate
Assesses ovarian blood flow when torsion is suspected -- needed urgently, not routinely

name: Ovarian cyst

triage.label: See a doctor soon
triage.action: Arrange an appointment in the next day or two

summary: A fluid-filled sac on an ovary, most commonly a benign functional cyst related to the normal menstrual cycle -- often entirely asymptomatic and found incidentally, but can cause one-sided lower abdominal/pelvic pain, either gradually or, if the cyst ruptures or the ovary twists (torsion), suddenly and severely. Most functional cysts resolve on their own within a few menstrual cycles without treatment. Sudden severe one-sided pain, especially with nausea/vomiting, needs urgent assessment to exclude ovarian torsion -- a genuine surgical emergency, distinct from the usual watch-and-wait approach for a simple cyst.
workup: Pelvic ultrasound -- the key investigation, characterises the cyst and guides management
Expectant management (repeat ultrasound in 6-8 weeks) for most simple, asymptomatic functional cysts -- genuinely as effective as active intervention for these
Urgent assessment for sudden severe one-sided pain with nausea/vomiting -- to exclude ovarian torsion, a surgical emergency
Gynaecology referral for cysts that are large, complex-looking on ultrasound, persistent beyond 2-3 cycles, or in a postmenopausal woman (higher malignancy concern at that age)

exam.step: Ask about pelvic pressure/fullness, and whether periods have become heavier or longer
exam.positive: The classic presenting pattern -- pressure symptoms and heavy bleeding, rather than acute pain

exam.step: Abdominal and pelvic examination for a palpable, non-tender pelvic mass or uterine enlargement
exam.positive: Larger fibroids may be palpable as a firm, irregular, non-tender mass

exam.step: Check for pallor and ask about fatigue -- signs of anaemia from associated heavy bleeding
exam.positive: A common, important consequence worth actively checking for, not just the pressure symptoms

labs.confirms: The key investigation -- confirms size, number and location of fibroids
Checks for iron-deficiency anaemia from associated heavy menstrual bleeding

name: Uterine fibroids

triage.label: Routine
triage.action: Discuss with your doctor at a routine appointment

summary: Benign smooth-muscle growths in the uterine wall -- extremely common (up to 70% of women by age 50), often entirely asymptomatic and found incidentally, but can cause a sensation of pelvic pressure/fullness, heavier or longer periods, and, if large, abdominal swelling. Gradually enlarging over months to years rather than a new acute problem. Iron-deficiency anaemia from associated heavy bleeding is a real, common consequence worth actively checking for, not just the pressure symptoms themselves.
workup: Pelvic ultrasound -- the key investigation, confirms size, number and location
Full blood count/ferritin to check for iron-deficiency anaemia from associated heavy bleeding
Expectant management for small, asymptomatic fibroids
Medical treatment (tranexamic acid, hormonal options) for bleeding symptoms
Gynaecology referral for large, rapidly growing, or significantly symptomatic fibroids -- myomectomy, uterine artery embolisation or hysterectomy are options depending on the individual situation

exam.step: Ask directly about the practical impact -- how often protection needs changing, passing large clots, periods lasting beyond 7 days
exam.positive: No evidence node captures 'heavy bleeding' directly -- this practical framing is how it is actually assessed in the history

exam.step: Check for pallor and ask about fatigue/breathlessness
exam.positive: Signs of the common, important consequence of iron-deficiency anaemia from ongoing heavy blood loss

exam.step: Ask whether the pattern is confined to the days of bleeding and recurs every cycle
exam.positive: Confirms a genuine cyclical menstrual problem rather than irregular/intermenstrual bleeding, which needs different assessment

labs.confirms: The most practically useful test -- confirms and quantifies iron-deficiency anaemia from the bleeding
Looks for a structural cause such as fibroids or polyps

name: Menorrhagia

triage.label: See a doctor soon
triage.action: Arrange an appointment in the next day or two

summary: Menstrual bleeding that is heavier and/or longer than typical -- soaking through usual protection every hour or two, passing large clots, or periods lasting more than 7 days -- recurring with each cycle. No dedicated evidence node exists anywhere in this checker for 'heavy bleeding' itself (the defining feature), so this is assessed through the downstream consequence of iron-deficiency anaemia (pallor, low ferritin) and the cyclical timing pattern, an honest, disclosed gap. Causes range from fibroids and hormonal imbalance to bleeding disorders -- persistent heavy bleeding deserves proper investigation, not just being told it's 'normal for you'.
workup: Full blood count and ferritin -- checks for the common, important consequence of iron-deficiency anaemia
Pelvic ultrasound to look for a structural cause (fibroids, polyps)
Tranexamic acid during bleeding days -- genuinely reduces blood loss
Hormonal options (combined pill, progestogen-releasing IUS) for ongoing control
Referral if bleeding is very heavy, associated with significant anaemia, or not responding to initial treatment

exam.step: Ask about hot flushes/night sweats disrupting sleep, and how long symptoms have been building
exam.positive: The classic pattern -- gradually developing over months as periods become irregular, though no dedicated evidence node captures flushes directly here

exam.step: Ask specifically about any bleeding after 12 months without a period
exam.positive: Postmenopausal bleeding is NOT a normal menopause symptom and needs assessment to exclude a gynaecological cause -- an important safety-netting question

exam.step: Ask about mood change, concentration ('brain fog'), and joint aches alongside the sleep disruption
exam.positive: Commonly co-occur with the hot flush/night sweat pattern, part of the same overall picture

labs.test: Clinical diagnosis based on age and symptom pattern
labs.confirms: Usually sufficient -- hormone testing is not routinely needed in a woman with typical symptoms at a typical age
Can support the diagnosis in atypical situations (e.g. younger age, uncertain picture), though not usually needed

name: Menopause

triage.label: Routine
triage.action: Discuss with your doctor at a routine appointment

summary: The natural transition marking the end of menstrual periods, typically age 45-55 -- hot flushes and night sweats (no dedicated evidence node exists for these directly; heat intolerance is used here as an imperfect proxy, a disclosed limitation) disrupting sleep, along with mood changes, 'brain fog', and joint aches, developing gradually over months as periods become irregular and then stop. A normal life transition, not a disease -- but genuinely disruptive symptoms are common and treatable, and shouldn't be dismissed. Bleeding after 12 months without a period (postmenopausal bleeding) is NOT a normal menopause symptom and needs assessment to exclude a gynaecological cause.
workup: Usually a clinical diagnosis based on age and symptom pattern -- hormone testing is not usually needed to diagnose menopause itself in a woman with typical symptoms at a typical age
Hormone replacement therapy (HRT) -- the most effective treatment for hot flushes/night sweats and genitourinary symptoms, for appropriately selected women without contraindications
Non-hormonal options (certain antidepressants, lifestyle measures) where HRT isn't suitable or preferred
Any bleeding after 12 months without a period needs assessment -- this is NOT a normal menopause symptom

exam.step: Ask specifically about itching alongside the discharge
exam.positive: Intense itching is the single most defining feature -- its relative absence should prompt reconsidering the diagnosis

exam.step: Ask about recent antibiotics, pregnancy, or known/poorly-controlled diabetes
exam.positive: Common, genuine triggers for an overgrowth of normally-present yeast, not sexual transmission

exam.step: Inspect for thick, white, curd-like ('cottage cheese') discharge and vulval redness
exam.positive: The classic appearance, distinct from the thinner, discoloured discharge of the other conditions in this bundle

labs.confirms: Usually sufficient given the classic itch + discharge pattern
Reserved for recurrent, atypical, or treatment-resistant cases to confirm the diagnosis and exclude another cause

name: Vaginal candidiasis

triage.label: Self-care
triage.action: This can usually be managed at home

summary: A very common overgrowth of Candida yeast (normally present in small amounts) causing intense vulval itching, soreness, and a thick, white, curd-like discharge -- NOT primarily sexually transmitted, unlike the other conditions sharing this bundle. Often triggered by recent antibiotics, pregnancy, or poorly-controlled diabetes. Recurrent episodes (4 or more a year) or symptoms not responding to standard treatment deserve proper assessment rather than repeated self-treatment, including a check for underlying diabetes.
workup: Usually a clinical diagnosis on the classic itch + discharge pattern
Over-the-counter or prescription antifungal (topical clotrimazole or oral fluconazole)
Avoid tight synthetic underwear and scented vaginal products, which can worsen irritation
Check blood glucose if episodes are recurrent -- poorly-controlled diabetes is a real, treatable trigger
Specialist referral for recurrent (4+ episodes/year) or treatment-resistant cases

exam.step: Ask specifically whether the discharge itches or is just noticed as an odour/appearance change
exam.positive: BV is classically NOT itchy -- a genuine distinguishing feature from candidiasis, the closest differential sharing this bundle

exam.step: Ask about a fishy odour, especially noticeable after sex
exam.positive: A characteristic, near-diagnostic feature of BV

exam.step: Inspect for a thin, greyish-white discharge coating the vaginal walls
exam.positive: The classic appearance, distinct from candidiasis's thick white discharge

labs.test: Clinical diagnosis (Amsel criteria) or vaginal pH testing
labs.confirms: Elevated vaginal pH (above 4.5) supports the diagnosis alongside the characteristic discharge and odour

labs.test: Vaginal swab microscopy (Gram stain, Nugent score)
labs.confirms: The laboratory gold standard when the diagnosis is uncertain

name: Bacterial vaginosis

triage.label: See a doctor soon
triage.action: Arrange an appointment in the next day or two

summary: An imbalance of normal vaginal bacteria producing a thin, greyish-white discharge with a characteristic fishy odour, often more noticeable after sex -- classically NOT itchy or sore, a genuine distinguishing feature from candidiasis. Not strictly classed as a sexually transmitted infection, though it is linked to sexual activity. Worth treating properly (not just masking the odour) since untreated BV genuinely raises the risk of pelvic infection and complications in pregnancy.
workup: Usually a clinical diagnosis on the discharge character and odour, sometimes supported by vaginal pH testing
Oral or vaginal metronidazole -- the standard, effective treatment
Avoid vaginal douching, which disrupts normal flora and can worsen or trigger BV
Treatment in pregnancy is genuinely important -- untreated BV is linked to preterm birth risk, so don't just tolerate the odour

exam.step: Inspect for a frothy, yellow-green, malodorous discharge
exam.positive: The classic appearance, distinct from candidiasis (white, curd-like) and BV (thin, greyish)

exam.step: Ask about a new or non-monogamous sexual partner, or a partner with symptoms
exam.positive: Trichomoniasis is a genuine STI -- unlike candidiasis/BV, sexual history is a real, relevant risk factor here

exam.step: Ask specifically about partner treatment when giving results/advice
exam.positive: Untreated partners lead to reinfection -- a genuinely important, sometimes overlooked management point

labs.confirms: The most sensitive test, now the standard confirmatory investigation
Can show motile trichomonads at the bedside, though less sensitive than NAAT

name: Trichomoniasis

triage.label: See a doctor soon
triage.action: Arrange an appointment in the next day or two

summary: A genuine sexually transmitted infection caused by the protozoan parasite Trichomonas vaginalis -- classically a frothy, yellow-green, malodorous discharge with vulval irritation and dysuria, though a substantial proportion of infections are mild or asymptomatic. Unlike candidiasis and bacterial vaginosis, this genuinely needs treating the sexual partner(s) too, or reinfection is very likely -- an important point patients are not always told.
workup: Vaginal swab NAAT (nucleic acid amplification test) -- the most sensitive confirmatory test
Oral metronidazole (single dose or a 7-day course, per current guidance) -- the standard, effective treatment
Treat sexual partner(s) at the same time, and avoid sex until both are treated and symptoms have resolved -- otherwise reinfection is very likely
Screen for other STIs, since co-infection is common

exam.step: Ask about dysuria, discharge (penile or vaginal), and any pelvic/testicular discomfort
exam.positive: The classic urethritis/cervicitis pattern, though genuinely often mild or absent -- a normal exam does not exclude infection

exam.step: Take a sexual history -- new/multiple partners, condom use, partner symptoms
exam.positive: The single most important risk-factor question for this condition specifically

exam.step: In women, examine for cervicitis (inflamed, friable cervix, mucopurulent discharge); in men, for urethral discharge
exam.positive: Supportive findings, though testing (not examination alone) confirms the diagnosis

labs.confirms: The standard, highly sensitive test for both organisms
Allows antibiotic susceptibility testing, important given rising resistance concerns

name: Gonorrhoea / Chlamydia

triage.label: See a doctor soon
triage.action: Arrange an appointment in the next day or two

summary: The two most common bacterial sexually transmitted infections -- causing urethritis/cervicitis with dysuria and discharge, though a genuinely large proportion of infections (especially chlamydia) are mild or entirely asymptomatic, which is exactly why they spread so easily and why opportunistic screening matters. Affects men and women. Left untreated, both can cause serious complications -- pelvic inflammatory disease and infertility risk in women, epididymitis in men -- so prompt treatment and partner notification genuinely matter, not just symptom relief.
workup: NAAT (nucleic acid amplification test) on a urine sample or swab -- the standard test for both infections
Ceftriaxone (single injection) for gonorrhoea, doxycycline (7-day course) for chlamydia, per current guidance -- treatment differs by organism, so testing before treating matters
Partner notification and treatment -- essential to prevent reinfection and interrupt onward spread
Screen for other STIs, since co-infection is common
Avoid sex until treatment is completed and partner(s) have also been treated

exam.step: Inspect for grouped, fluid-filled blisters progressing to shallow, painful ulcers in the genital area
exam.positive: The classic appearance -- deliberately compared with Shingles's dermatomal vesicles already modelled in this bundle, though herpes is not confined to a single dermatome

exam.step: Ask whether this is a first episode or a recurrence, and about any fever/flu-like symptoms
exam.positive: First episodes are typically more severe and more likely to have systemic symptoms than recurrences

exam.step: Take a sexual history and discuss partner disclosure
exam.positive: Relevant for risk-factor assessment and for the ongoing management conversation, though no dedicated evidence node captures sexual history directly in this bundle

labs.confirms: Often sufficient given the characteristic appearance

labs.test: Viral PCR or culture of a lesion swab
labs.confirms: Confirms the diagnosis and distinguishes HSV-1 from HSV-2 when uncertain

name: Genital herpes

triage.label: See a doctor soon
triage.action: Arrange an appointment in the next day or two

summary: A common sexually transmitted viral infection causing painful, grouped, fluid-filled blisters that break down into shallow ulcers, typically in the genital area. A first episode is often the most severe, sometimes with fever and flu-like symptoms; recurrences are usually milder and shorter. This is a lifelong infection (the virus remains dormant between outbreaks) -- an important point for a first diagnosis conversation, alongside the fact that outbreaks typically become less frequent and severe over time with appropriate management.
workup: Usually a clinical diagnosis on the characteristic grouped vesicles/ulcers, confirmed with viral PCR/culture of a swab if uncertain
Oral antiviral (aciclovir, valaciclovir or famciclovir) for the first episode -- most effective if started early
Suppressive daily antiviral therapy for people with frequent recurrences, or to reduce transmission risk to a partner
Discuss disclosure and transmission-risk-reduction with sexual partner(s)

exam.step: Ask specifically whether the rash itches
exam.positive: Syphilis's rash is classically NON-itchy -- a genuine, clinically-taught negative discriminator against nearly every other rash-producing condition

exam.step: Inspect the palms and soles specifically
exam.positive: Involvement here is a distinctive, easily-overlooked feature of secondary syphilis

exam.step: Ask about a preceding painless genital ulcer weeks earlier, and check for generalised lymphadenopathy and mucous patches
exam.positive: The classic sequence -- primary chancre followed weeks later by the secondary-stage rash -- though no dedicated evidence node captures the primary chancre directly here

labs.confirms: Used for both initial screening and monitoring treatment response over time
Confirms the diagnosis, remaining positive for life even after successful treatment

name: Syphilis

triage.label: Urgent
triage.action: Seek medical assessment today

summary: A sexually transmitted bacterial infection progressing through distinct stages. This models the SECONDARY stage specifically -- a widespread, classically NON-ITCHY rash (often including the palms and soles, a genuinely distinctive feature), sometimes with fever, generalised lymphadenopathy and mucous patches, appearing weeks after an initial, often-painless genital ulcer (the primary chancre, for which no dedicated evidence node exists here -- a disclosed gap). Untreated syphilis progresses through further stages with serious long-term complications, which is exactly why prompt diagnosis and treatment genuinely matter, not just symptom relief.
workup: Serological testing (treponemal and non-treponemal tests) -- the standard diagnostic approach
A single intramuscular injection of benzathine penicillin G for early syphilis -- highly effective and still first-line
Partner notification and testing -- essential given ongoing transmission risk
HIV testing at the same visit -- co-infection is genuinely common and both need addressing
Follow-up serology to confirm treatment response

exam.step: Ask about a flu-like illness with fever, sore throat, rash and swollen glands 2-4 weeks after a specific exposure risk
exam.positive: The classic acute seroconversion pattern, though many people have no symptoms at all at this stage

exam.step: Take a careful, non-judgemental sexual/exposure history
exam.positive: The single most important step for deciding whether testing is indicated -- no dedicated evidence node captures exposure history directly in this bundle

exam.step: Examine for generalised lymphadenopathy and any rash
exam.positive: Supportive findings in acute seroconversion, though their absence does not exclude infection

labs.confirms: The standard screening test -- detects acute infection earlier than older antibody-only tests

labs.test: HIV viral load and confirmatory testing
labs.confirms: Confirms the diagnosis and guides urgent referral to start antiretroviral therapy

name: HIV / AIDS

triage.label: See a doctor soon
triage.action: Arrange an appointment in the next day or two

summary: This models the ACUTE SEROCONVERSION illness -- a flu-like syndrome with fever, generalised lymphadenopathy, malaise, sometimes a rash and night sweats, occurring 2-4 weeks after exposure -- since this is the presentation most likely to prompt someone to seek care. Many people have no symptoms at all at this stage, and the chronic, often-asymptomatic course that follows for years is not well captured by any single symptom cluster, a genuine, disclosed limitation of a symptom-based checker for this condition. With modern antiretroviral therapy, HIV is a manageable chronic condition with a normal life expectancy when treated -- testing after any genuine exposure risk, not waiting for symptoms, is how this is actually caught early.
workup: HIV antigen/antibody combination test -- the standard screening test, detects acute infection earlier than antibody-only tests
Confirmatory testing and viral load if the screening test is positive

Prompt referral to start antiretroviral therapy (ART) if confirmed -- modern ART gives a normal life expectancy and, with an undetectable viral load, means the virus cannot be sexually transmitted ('undetectable = untransmittable')
Screen for other STIs, since co-infection (especially with syphilis) is common
Post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) if within 72 hours of a specific high-risk exposure, or pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) for ongoing risk reduction

exam.step: Inspect and palpate the neck for a visible or palpable, generally symmetric thyroid enlargement
exam.positive: No dedicated evidence node captures visible neck swelling directly here -- this is assessed on examination, the actual presenting complaint

exam.step: Ask specifically about weight change, heat/cold intolerance, and mood -- looking for their ABSENCE
exam.positive: Simple goitre is usually euthyroid -- their absence supports this over Hypothyroidism/Hyperthyroidism sharing this bundle

exam.step: Assess dietary iodine intake (use of iodised salt, regional iodine-deficiency risk)
exam.positive: The genuine, correctable underlying cause in much of India

labs.confirms: Confirms normal thyroid function, distinguishing simple goitre from over/under-active thyroid disease
Characterises the gland and any nodules if the enlargement is asymmetric or rapidly progressive

name: Goitre (simple/iodine-deficiency)

triage.label: Routine
triage.action: Discuss with your doctor at a routine appointment

summary: A visible or palpable enlargement of the thyroid gland, most commonly from dietary iodine deficiency -- a genuinely significant public health issue in parts of India, particularly the Himalayan belt and other iodine-deficient regions. Unlike Hypothyroidism/Hyperthyroidism sharing this bundle, simple goitre is usually EUTHYROID (normal thyroid function) -- no weight change, temperature intolerance or mood change, since the gland is simply enlarged, not over- or under-active. No dedicated 'visible neck swelling' evidence node exists anywhere in this checker -- the actual presenting complaint -- so this is assessed on examination rather than a specific symptom question.
workup: Thyroid function tests (TSH, T4) -- to confirm the gland is functioning normally, distinguishing simple goitre from Hypothyroidism/Hyperthyroidism
Urinary iodine estimation where iodine deficiency is suspected
Iodised salt and correcting dietary iodine intake -- the standard public-health and individual measure
Ultrasound and/or referral if the gland is rapidly enlarging, hard, or asymmetric, to exclude a nodule needing separate assessment

exam.step: Review OGTT results against pregnancy-specific diagnostic thresholds

name: Premenstrual syndrome
